title: Java Interview Questions and Answers (Core Java, Collections, Concurrency)
description: Hundreds of Java interview questions with detailed answers and code: OOP, collections, concurrency, JVM and garbage collection, streams, Spring and more. Free sample, practice and revise.
intro: Java interviews test three things: how well you know the language (OOP, collections, generics, exceptions, streams), how you reason about concurrency and memory (threads, locks, the Java memory model, garbage collection), and how you apply it to real services (Spring, databases, performance). The questions below cover all three, each with a worked answer and code.

Start with the fundamentals, then move to concurrency and JVM internals, which is where mid-level and senior interviews spend most of their time. Mark what you have read, revise what you missed, and use the coding problems to practise the same ideas under a timer.

faq.q: What are the most asked Java interview topics?
faq.a: Object-oriented design, the collections framework (HashMap internals especially), multithreading and the java.util.concurrent package, exceptions, the JVM memory model and garbage collection, Java 8 streams and lambdas, and Spring for backend roles.

faq.q: How should I prepare for a Java interview in a week?
faq.a: Spend the first days on collections, OOP and exceptions, then concurrency and JVM internals, and finish with a few coding problems and one design question. Reading each answer and then explaining it aloud works better than rereading.

faq.q: Do I need to know Spring for a Java interview?
faq.a: For most backend roles, yes: dependency injection, how a request flows through a Spring Boot application, transactions and configuration. See the Spring Boot questions linked on this page.

faq.q: Are these Java questions free?
faq.a: A sample is free to read without paying. Create a free account to unlock more, and Premium unlocks every answer.

title: Spring Boot Interview Questions and Answers
description: Spring Boot interview questions with clear answers: auto-configuration, dependency injection, REST controllers, transactions, JPA, security, testing and production issues.
h1: Spring Boot Interview Questions and Answers
intro: Spring Boot interviews go beyond annotations. Interviewers want to know how auto-configuration decides which beans to create, how dependency injection and bean scopes behave, what a transaction boundary really covers, and how you would debug a slow or failing endpoint in production.

The questions below are the Spring-related ones from our Java collection. Read the answer, then try to explain the mechanism in your own words: that is the difference between knowing the annotation and understanding the framework.

faq.q: What is Spring Boot auto-configuration?
faq.a: It creates beans automatically based on what is on the classpath and on your properties, using conditional configuration, so a starter dependency is usually enough to get a working component.

faq.q: What do interviewers ask about Spring transactions?
faq.a: Where the transaction boundary is, why a self-invocation inside the same class skips the proxy, propagation and isolation levels, and how rollback works for checked and unchecked exceptions.

faq.q: How do I prepare for Spring Boot questions quickly?
faq.a: Build or review one small REST service end to end (controller, service, repository, a transaction, a test), then read the questions here and explain each mechanism aloud.

title: LLD Interview Questions: Low-Level Design and Design Patterns
description: Low-level design (LLD) interview questions with answers: design patterns, SOLID principles, class design and object-oriented modelling, with code examples.
intro: Low-level design rounds ask you to turn a small problem (a parking lot, an elevator, a rate limiter) into clean classes and interfaces. Interviewers look for sensible responsibilities, the right design pattern used for the right reason, extensibility without rewrites, and code that is easy to test.

These questions cover the design patterns (creational, structural, behavioural) and the principles behind them, with code. Learn when a pattern helps and when it is over-engineering; that judgement is what gets scored.

faq.q: What is the difference between LLD and HLD?
faq.a: High-level design is about the whole system: services, databases, queues, scale. Low-level design is about the code inside one component: classes, interfaces, patterns and their relationships.

faq.q: Which design patterns are asked most often?
faq.a: Singleton, Factory, Builder, Strategy, Observer, Decorator and State come up most, along with the SOLID principles.

faq.q: How do I practise LLD?
faq.a: Pick a classic problem, list the requirements, sketch the classes and interfaces, then code the core flow. Compare with the answers here and notice what you would change.

title: SDE-2 Interview Preparation: DSA, System Design, LLD and Behavioral
description: A practical SDE-2 interview preparation plan: what to study for DSA, system design (HLD), low-level design, language depth and behavioral rounds, with questions and roadmaps.
intro: An SDE-2 (mid-level) interview usually has four parts: data structures and algorithms, a system design round, a low-level design or machine-coding round, and a behavioral round about ownership and decisions. The bar rises on design and on how you communicate trade-offs, not only on solving the problem.

A workable plan: two to three weeks of DSA patterns (sliding window, two pointers, trees, graphs, dynamic programming), a week each on HLD and LLD with a few full designs spoken aloud, and the last days on behavioral stories and company-specific preparation.

links.label: Solo system design practice, scored out of 10

faq.q: How is an SDE-2 interview different from SDE-1?
faq.a: More weight on system design and design trade-offs, on owning a feature end to end, and on communication. Coding problems are still there, usually at a medium to hard level.

faq.q: How long should I prepare for SDE-2?
faq.a: Most people need six to eight weeks alongside a job. Spend the first weeks on DSA patterns and the rest on design and company-specific rounds.

faq.q: What system design topics matter most?
faq.a: Scaling reads and writes, caching, sharding and replication, queues and event-driven design, consistency trade-offs, and designing common systems such as a URL shortener, a chat app, a feed and a rate limiter.

title: Amazon SDE-2 Interview: Rounds, Questions and Preparation
description: How the Amazon SDE-2 interview works: coding, system design, low-level design and leadership principles, with Amazon-tagged coding problems and a preparation plan.
intro: Amazon's SDE-2 loop typically combines coding rounds, a system design round, and behavioral questions built around the Leadership Principles (ownership, customer obsession, dive deep, deliver results). Expect to be asked for specific stories with measurable outcomes.

Prepare on three tracks: Amazon-tagged coding problems for the DSA rounds, a handful of full system designs you can talk through for 45 minutes, and eight to ten behavioral stories mapped to the principles. The problems listed below are the ones reported for Amazon.

links.label: Amazon interview roadmap, round by round

faq.q: What are the rounds in the Amazon SDE-2 interview?
faq.a: Usually an online assessment, then a loop of coding, system design and behavioral rounds, including a bar-raiser. The exact format changes by team, so check your recruiter's schedule.

faq.q: How important are the Leadership Principles?
faq.a: Very. Every round can include behavioral questions, and strong technical answers do not make up for missing stories. Prepare specific examples with numbers.

faq.q: What DSA topics does Amazon ask?
faq.a: Arrays and strings, hash maps, trees and graphs, sliding window and two pointers, heaps, and dynamic programming at a medium level are the most common.

title: Kafka Interview Questions and Answers (Beginner to Advanced)
description: Kafka interview questions with answers: partitions, consumer groups, offsets, delivery guarantees, exactly-once, replication, retention and production troubleshooting.
intro: Kafka interviews start with the model (topics, partitions, offsets, consumer groups) and quickly move to guarantees and failure: what happens when a consumer is slower than the producer, how ordering works across partitions, what exactly-once really means, and how replication and leader election keep data safe.

The questions below run from basics to production scenarios such as lag, rebalances, retries and backpressure. Learn the trade-offs, not only the definitions: they are what senior interviewers ask about.

faq.q: What is a consumer group in Kafka?
faq.a: A set of consumers that share a topic's partitions, so each partition is read by exactly one consumer in the group. It is how Kafka scales consumption while keeping per-partition ordering.

faq.q: Does Kafka guarantee ordering?
faq.a: Only within a partition. If you need ordering for related events, give them the same key so they go to the same partition.

faq.q: What does exactly-once mean in Kafka?
faq.a: With idempotent producers and transactions, a message is written once and a consume-process-produce chain can commit atomically. It does not make external side effects exactly-once by itself.

title: Sliding Window LeetCode Problems: Patterns and Practice
description: Sliding window problems for coding interviews: fixed and variable window patterns, when to use them, and a list of problems you can run online.
h1: Sliding Window Problems for Coding Interviews
intro: Sliding window turns many O(n squared) subarray and substring problems into O(n). Keep two pointers that mark a window, grow it on the right, and shrink it from the left while a condition is broken. There are two common shapes: a fixed-size window (maximum sum of k elements) and a variable-size window (longest substring without repeating characters).

To recognise it, look for words like longest, shortest, subarray, substring, contiguous, at most k. Write down what the window must satisfy and what you update when it moves, then code the loop. The problems below are tagged with this pattern and run online.

faq.q: When should I use a sliding window?
faq.a: When you need the best contiguous subarray or substring under a condition, and extending or shrinking the range changes the answer in a predictable way.

faq.q: What is the difference between fixed and variable windows?
faq.a: A fixed window has a set size and slides one step at a time. A variable window grows until a condition breaks, then shrinks from the left until it holds again.

faq.q: What is the time complexity?
faq.a: Usually O(n), because each pointer moves forward at most n times, plus any cost of the structure you keep for the window, such as a hash map.

A good order is to start with the small designs (URL shortener, rate limiter, notification service) to learn the building blocks, then do the data-heavy ones (feed, chat, search), and leave payments and multi-region for last. Say each design out loud once before you read the answer.

faq.q: How do I start a system design answer?
faq.a: Ask what the system must do and how big it is, write down the numbers (users, requests per second, storage), then sketch the simplest design that works and improve it where the numbers say it will break.

faq.q: How much detail do interviewers expect?
faq.a: Enough to defend each box: what it stores, how it scales and what happens when it fails. A short, correct design with clear trade-offs beats a long diagram you cannot explain.

faq.q: Can I practise without a partner?
faq.a: Yes. The practice page lets you answer a question by typing or speaking and scores how much of a strong design you covered. Your first three scored questions are free.

title: Dynamic Programming Interview Problems with Solutions
description: Dynamic programming interview problems from real company interviews, with solutions. Learn to spot the state, write the recurrence and cut the space.
intro: Dynamic programming looks hard because the answer is usually short but the thinking is not. For each problem, ask three things: what is the smallest version of this question, what choices do I have at each step, and which earlier answers do I need to combine.

Start with the one-dimensional problems (climbing stairs, house robber, coin change), then move to two-dimensional grids and strings, and do knapsack and interval problems last. Write the recurrence in words before you write any code.

faq.q: How do I know a problem needs dynamic programming?
faq.a: You are asked for a count, a minimum or a maximum, and a brute-force search would repeat the same sub-problems. If a recursive solution calls itself with the same arguments more than once, memoise it.

faq.q: Top-down or bottom-up?
faq.a: Write the recursive version with memoisation first because it matches how you think. Convert to a table only if the interviewer asks for it or the recursion is too deep.

title: Graph Interview Problems: BFS, DFS, Shortest Path and Union-Find
description: Graph interview problems from company interviews with solutions: BFS, DFS, topological sort, shortest paths and union-find, grouped so you can practise one pattern at a time.
intro: Most graph problems in interviews are one of four things in disguise: reachability (DFS or BFS), shortest path in an unweighted grid (BFS), ordering with dependencies (topological sort) or connecting groups (union-find). The skill is spotting which one, since the graph is often hidden in a grid or a list of pairs.
Practise building the adjacency list yourself, because that is where most bugs are. Then decide how you will mark visited nodes before you write the traversal.

faq.q: BFS or DFS for a grid problem?
faq.a: BFS when you need the shortest number of steps, DFS when you only need to know whether something is reachable or to count connected regions.

faq.q: When do I use union-find?
faq.a: When you keep merging groups and repeatedly ask whether two items are in the same group, for example connected components or detecting a cycle in an undirected graph.

title: React Interview Questions and Answers (Hooks, State, Performance)
description: Practical React interview questions with answers: components and props, hooks, state management, rendering and reconciliation, performance and testing. Free sample, then practise and revise.
intro: React interviews start with how components render and re-render: props versus state, keys, the virtual DOM and reconciliation, and what actually triggers an update. Interviewers then push into hooks (useState, useEffect, useMemo, useCallback, useRef), their rules, and the bugs they cause: stale closures, missing dependencies and effect loops.

Senior rounds move to design: state management trade-offs (context versus a store), data fetching and caching, code splitting, memoisation that really helps, accessibility and testing. Each question below has a worked answer with a short code example, so you can explain the why and not only the what.

faq.q: What React topics are asked most in interviews?
faq.a: Hooks and their pitfalls, how rendering and reconciliation work, state management (lifting state, context, stores), performance (memoisation, lists, code splitting) and testing components.

faq.q: How do I prepare for a React interview?
faq.a: Build one small app that uses every common hook, then read the answers here and explain each one out loud. Practise spotting a stale closure or an unnecessary re-render in a code snippet.

faq.q: Are class components still asked?
faq.a: Occasionally, mostly to compare the lifecycle with hooks. Focus on function components, but know how componentDidMount, componentDidUpdate and componentWillUnmount map to useEffect.

title: Node.js Interview Questions and Answers (Event Loop, Streams, Async)
description: Node.js interview questions with detailed answers: the event loop, async patterns, streams, clustering, error handling, security and performance. Free sample, practise and revise.
intro: Node.js interviews revolve around one idea: a single thread running an event loop. You are expected to explain the phases of the loop, the difference between process.nextTick, microtasks and timers, why blocking the loop is dangerous, and how callbacks, promises and async/await relate.

Beyond the loop, expect streams and backpressure, the cluster and worker-thread modules, memory leaks, error handling in async code, security basics (injection, rate limiting, dependency risk) and how you would structure and scale an Express or Fastify service. The answers below include runnable examples.

faq.q: What is the event loop in Node.js?
faq.a: It is the mechanism that lets a single thread handle many connections: it runs callbacks from queues in phases (timers, pending, poll, check, close) and drains microtasks between them, handing slow work to the operating system or a thread pool.

faq.q: When should I use worker threads or cluster?
faq.a: Use cluster to run several processes that share a port and use all CPU cores for I/O-heavy servers. Use worker threads for CPU-heavy work inside one process so the event loop is not blocked.

faq.q: What Node.js topics are asked at senior level?
faq.a: Scaling and observability, memory leaks and profiling, streams and backpressure, graceful shutdown, security hardening and designing resilient services.

title: SQL Interview Questions and Answers (Joins, Indexes, Transactions)
description: SQL interview questions with worked answers: joins, group by and having, window functions, indexes and query plans, transactions and isolation levels, normalisation and design.
intro: SQL screens begin with query fluency: the join types and when each is right, GROUP BY with HAVING, subqueries versus CTEs, and window functions such as ROW_NUMBER, RANK and running totals. You are usually given a small schema and asked to write the query, then to explain its cost.

Deeper rounds cover how the database executes a query: indexes (B-tree, composite, covering), reading an execution plan, why a query is slow, transactions, ACID and isolation levels (dirty reads, phantom reads, deadlocks), and normalisation versus denormalisation for real workloads.

faq.q: What SQL topics come up most in interviews?
faq.a: Joins, aggregation with GROUP BY and HAVING, window functions, subqueries and CTEs, indexing and query plans, transactions and isolation levels, and schema design.

faq.q: What is the difference between WHERE and HAVING?
faq.a: WHERE filters rows before grouping; HAVING filters groups after aggregation, so it can use aggregate functions like COUNT or SUM.

faq.q: How do I make a slow query faster?
faq.a: Read the execution plan, check that filters and joins can use an index, avoid functions on indexed columns, select only the columns you need and consider a covering or composite index.

title: Go (Golang) Interview Questions and Answers (Goroutines, Channels)
description: Go interview questions with answers: goroutines and channels, the scheduler, interfaces, error handling, context, memory and garbage collection, and testing. Free sample, practise and revise.
intro: Go interviews test whether you think in Go: small interfaces, composition over inheritance, explicit error values and zero values that are useful. Expect questions on slices versus arrays, maps, pointers, defer, panic and recover, and how method sets and interfaces interact.

Concurrency is the centre of gravity: goroutines and the scheduler, channels (buffered and unbuffered), select, sync primitives, the context package for cancellation and deadlines, data races and how to find them. Senior rounds add profiling, memory and garbage collection, and structuring services.

faq.q: What is a goroutine?
faq.a: A lightweight function execution managed by the Go runtime scheduler, not by the operating system. Thousands can run on a few OS threads because they start small and are multiplexed.

faq.q: Buffered versus unbuffered channels?
faq.a: An unbuffered channel makes sender and receiver meet (synchronise); a buffered channel lets senders continue until the buffer is full.

faq.q: How do you avoid data races in Go?
faq.a: Share memory by communicating over channels, protect shared state with sync.Mutex or atomic operations, and run tests with the race detector (go test -race).

title: Microservices Interview Questions and Answers (Saga, Circuit Breaker)
description: Microservices interview questions with answers: service boundaries, communication, API gateway, saga and eventual consistency, resilience patterns, observability and deployment.
intro: Microservices interviews are about trade-offs, not definitions. You should be able to say when a monolith is the better choice, how to draw service boundaries around business capabilities, and what you pay for the split: network failures, data consistency, versioning and operational overhead.

Expect the standard toolkit: synchronous versus asynchronous communication, the API gateway, service discovery, the circuit breaker, retries with backoff, bulkheads, the saga pattern for distributed transactions, idempotency, distributed tracing and centralised logging. These answers explain each one with its failure mode.

faq.q: When should you not use microservices?
faq.a: When the team is small, the domain is still changing, or you cannot invest in deployment, monitoring and testing automation. A well-structured monolith is often faster to build and easier to run.

faq.q: How do you handle a transaction across services?
faq.a: Avoid it by design where you can. Otherwise use the saga pattern: a sequence of local transactions with compensating actions, coordinated by choreography (events) or orchestration (a coordinator).

faq.q: What is a circuit breaker?
faq.a: A guard around a remote call that stops calling a failing service after repeated errors, fails fast, and tries again after a cool-down so the failure does not cascade.

title: Angular Interview Questions and Answers (RxJS, DI, Change Detection)
description: Angular interview questions with answers: components and modules, dependency injection, change detection, RxJS and observables, routing, forms and performance. Free sample, practise and revise.
intro: Angular interviews check that you understand the framework's building blocks: components, templates and data binding, directives, pipes, services and dependency injection, modules versus standalone components, and the component lifecycle hooks.

The harder questions concern behaviour: how change detection works and when OnPush helps, RxJS operators (switchMap, mergeMap, debounceTime) and unsubscribing, reactive versus template-driven forms, route guards and lazy loading, and how you would test and optimise a large application.

faq.q: What is change detection in Angular?
faq.a: The process that checks component data against the template and updates the DOM. By default it checks every component after each event; OnPush limits it to input changes and explicit triggers.

faq.q: switchMap versus mergeMap?
faq.a: switchMap cancels the previous inner observable when a new value arrives (good for search-as-you-type); mergeMap runs them all in parallel.

faq.q: How do I prepare for an Angular interview?
faq.a: Know DI, change detection and RxJS well, build a small app with routing and reactive forms, and be ready to explain how you would optimise a slow screen.

title: Ruby on Rails Interview Questions and Answers (ActiveRecord, MVC)
description: Ruby on Rails interview questions with answers: MVC, ActiveRecord and associations, N+1 queries, callbacks, background jobs, caching, security and testing.
h1: Ruby on Rails Interview Questions and Answers
intro: Rails interviews test convention-over-configuration thinking: how a request flows through routes, controllers, models and views, how ActiveRecord maps tables and associations, validations, scopes and migrations, and when callbacks help or hurt.

Performance and production topics follow: the N+1 query problem and eager loading, database indexes, caching layers, background jobs, security defaults (strong parameters, CSRF, SQL injection) and test strategy. Senior rounds ask how you would structure a large Rails app and keep models thin.

faq.q: What is the N+1 query problem?
faq.a: Loading a list of records and then querying once per record for an association. Fix it with eager loading (includes, preload or eager_load) so the associations load in one or two queries.

faq.q: Are callbacks bad practice?
faq.a: Not by themselves, but business logic hidden in callbacks is hard to test and reason about. Prefer explicit service objects for multi-step workflows and keep callbacks for simple, local concerns.

faq.q: How do you keep Rails controllers thin?
faq.a: Move business logic into models or service objects, use strong parameters and concerns for shared behaviour, and keep the controller to authentication, parameters and the response.

title: AWS Interview Questions and Answers (EC2, S3, IAM, VPC)
description: AWS interview questions with answers: EC2, S3, IAM, VPC networking, Lambda, databases, scaling and the Well-Architected pillars. Free sample, practise and revise.
intro: AWS interviews start with the core services and when to choose each: EC2 and auto scaling, S3 storage classes and consistency, IAM users, roles and policies, VPC subnets, route tables and security groups, load balancers, and managed databases such as RDS and DynamoDB.

Senior rounds ask you to design on AWS: high availability across availability zones, cost control, serverless with Lambda and API Gateway, queues and event-driven designs (SQS, SNS, EventBridge), monitoring with CloudWatch, and security best practice such as least privilege and encryption.

faq.q: What is the difference between a security group and a network ACL?
faq.a: A security group is a stateful firewall at the instance level; a network ACL is a stateless firewall at the subnet level, with separate inbound and outbound rules.

faq.q: When would you use Lambda instead of EC2?
faq.a: For short, event-driven or spiky workloads where you do not want to manage servers. Use EC2 for long-running processes, special hardware or predictable steady load.

faq.q: How do you make an application highly available on AWS?
faq.a: Run across multiple availability zones behind a load balancer, use auto scaling, keep state in managed multi-AZ services, and test failover.

title: Behavioral Interview Questions and Answers (STAR Method, Leadership)
description: Behavioral interview questions with sample answers: conflict, failure, leadership, ownership, ambiguity and teamwork, using the STAR method. Free sample, practise and revise.
intro: Behavioral rounds ask for evidence, not opinions: a specific time you resolved a conflict, handled failure, led without authority, disagreed with a decision or delivered under ambiguity. The STAR structure (situation, task, action, result) keeps answers short and concrete.

Strong answers name your own actions (not the team's), include a measurable result and end with what you learned. Prepare six to eight stories that can each answer several questions, and map them to the company's stated values. The examples below show how to shape them.

faq.q: What is the STAR method?
faq.a: A way to structure a story: Situation and Task set the context briefly, Action is what you did, and Result is the outcome with numbers where possible.

faq.q: How many stories should I prepare?
faq.a: Six to eight strong ones, covering conflict, failure, leadership, ownership, ambiguity and a technical achievement. One story can often answer several questions.

faq.q: How do I answer a question about a failure?
faq.a: Pick a real, bounded failure, own your part, explain what you changed afterwards and show the improved result. Avoid blaming others or choosing a fake weakness.

The patterns that unlock most of them are two pointers, sliding window, prefix sums, in-place swaps and sorting first. Learn to recognise which pattern a statement hints at before writing any code.

Practise by reading the constraints: a sorted input suggests two pointers or binary search; a subarray with a sum or length condition suggests a sliding window or prefix sums; in-place with O(1) space suggests swapping and index tricks. intro: String problems test careful indexing and the right data structure: a hash map of counts, two pointers for palindromes, a sliding window for substrings and a stack for brackets. Know how your language stores strings, because immutability changes the cost of building them.

Common themes are anagrams, palindromes, longest substring conditions, parsing and matching. Practise stating the complexity of your solution and the edge cases (empty string, one character, repeated characters). Open any problem to run your code against test cases.

title: Hash Table Problems from Real Interviews, with Solutions
description: Hash Table coding problems asked in real interviews at top companies: practise online in 11 languages with test cases, and see the pattern behind each one.
h1: Hash Table Problems for Coding Interviews
intro: A hash table trades memory for speed: constant-time lookups turn many quadratic solutions into linear ones. The classic uses are counting frequencies, finding a complement (two sum), grouping by a key and detecting duplicates or cycles.

When a brute-force solution compares every pair, ask whether remembering what you have already seen would let you answer in one pass. Practise choosing the right key, handling collisions in your explanation and bounding the memory you use.

title: Tree Problems from Real Interviews, with Solutions
description: Tree coding problems asked in real interviews at top companies: practise online in 11 languages with test cases, and see the pattern behind each one.
intro: Tree problems reward recursion: define what a function returns for one node assuming its children are solved, then combine. Depth-first traversals (pre-order, in-order, post-order) and breadth-first level order cover most questions.

Know the properties of a binary search tree, how to compute height, diameter and lowest common ancestor, and how to serialise a tree. Practise writing both the recursive and the iterative version and stating the space cost of the call stack.

title: Backtracking Problems from Real Interviews, with Solutions
description: Backtracking coding problems asked in real interviews at top companies: practise online in 11 languages with test cases, and see the pattern behind each one.
intro: Backtracking builds a solution step by step and undoes a choice when it cannot lead to an answer. It is the tool for permutations, combinations, subsets, board puzzles and constraint problems, where you must explore many possibilities.

The template is choose, explore, un-choose. The skill is pruning: stop early when a partial solution already breaks a rule, and avoid repeated work by sorting or skipping duplicates. Practise estimating the size of the search space.

title: Binary Search Problems from Real Interviews, with Solutions
description: Binary Search coding problems asked in real interviews at top companies: practise online in 11 languages with test cases, and see the pattern behind each one.
h1: Binary Search Problems for Coding Interviews
intro: Binary search is not only for sorted arrays: it works whenever you can test a yes or no condition that flips exactly once. That includes searching an answer range (minimum capacity, smallest speed) as well as finding a position.

Most bugs come from off-by-one boundaries. Fix a convention (inclusive or exclusive bounds, which half to keep) and use it every time. Practise lower bound, upper bound, rotated arrays and search on the answer.

h1: Linked List Problems for Coding Interviews
intro: Linked list questions test pointer handling under pressure: reversing a list, detecting a cycle, merging sorted lists and finding the middle. A dummy head node and the fast and slow pointer technique remove most of the special cases.

Draw the pointers before coding and update them in the right order so you never lose the rest of the list. Practise doing each task in one pass and O(1) extra space, and test the empty list and single node.

h1: Two Pointers Problems for Coding Interviews
intro: Two pointers turns a quadratic scan into a linear one by moving two indexes through the data with a rule for which one advances. It works on sorted arrays, on palindromes and when partitioning in place.

Decide what each pointer means and why the move is safe (it never skips a better answer). Practise the variants: opposite ends, same direction (fast and slow) and one pointer reading while the other writes.

title: Greedy Problems from Real Interviews, with Solutions
description: Greedy coding problems asked in real interviews at top companies: practise online in 11 languages with test cases, and see the pattern behind each one.
intro: A greedy algorithm makes the best local choice at each step and never revisits it. It is correct only when a local optimum leads to a global one, so the interview is about justifying the choice, usually with an exchange argument.

Typical problems are interval scheduling, jump game, gas station and assigning resources. Practise sorting by the right key, then compare with a dynamic programming solution to see why the greedy one is valid or fails.

description: Bit Manipulation coding problems asked in real interviews at top companies: practise online in 11 languages with test cases, and see the pattern behind each one.
h1: Bit Manipulation Problems for Coding Interviews
intro: Bit manipulation uses the binary form of numbers for compact state and fast tricks: XOR to find the odd one out, masks for subsets, shifts for powers of two and counting set bits. Many problems that look like maths reduce to a bitwise identity.

Know the operators and their precedence, how negative numbers are stored and how to test, set and clear a bit. Practise single number, counting bits, power of two and subset enumeration with a bitmask.
